```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# Each fit below takes about an hour (97,806 one-minute occasions), so the
# fitting code is not run when the vignette is built. The results were saved
# by dev/precompute-curiango.R and are read from curiango-fits.rds.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "100%")
library(crywolf)
fits <- readRDS("curiango-fits.rds")
classifiers <- c(custom = "Custom", birdnet = "BirdNET")
model_labels <- c(standard = "standard", constant = "constant rate",
                  covariates = "rate on covariates")
fits <- fits[paste(rep(names(classifiers), each = 3), names(model_labels),
                   sep = "_")]
row_of <- function(f, var) f$table[f$table$variable == var, ]
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * x)
```

```{r stale, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(crywolf:::.stale_note(fits, "curiango-fits.rds"))
```

This article fits the models of `vignette("crywolf")` to real data: passive
acoustic monitoring of the Common Pauraque (*Nyctidromus albicollis*) at
seven sites in the Pantanal and adjacent Cerrado, Brazil (Piatti et al.,
2026). Two automated classifiers scored every one-minute recording, a custom
model and BirdNET (Kahl et al., 2021), and an independent sample of about 1%
of the recordings was annotated by ear. The annotated recordings are the
verified method of the multiple-methods design (Miller et al., 2011).

We ask three questions. How often does each classifier produce a false
positive? Do the environmental effects on occupancy change when false
positives are modelled? And does the false-positive rate itself depend on
the environment?

## The data

`curiango` is a list with one table of recordings, one of site-nights, and
one of annotated recordings:

```{r data}
str(curiango, max.level = 1)
```

The occupancy unit is the site-night (whether the species called that
night) and the occasion is the one-minute recording. A recording is an
automated detection when the classifier's confidence score reaches a
threshold; we use the thresholds that maximized F1 in Piatti et al. (2026),
0.40 for the custom classifier and 0.10 for BirdNET. Nightly temperature,
relative humidity, and the log of lunar illumination enter the occupancy
model, standardized. The Bioacoustic Index (`bio`) and the Acoustic
Complexity Index (`aci`) of each recording enter the true-detection model,
and each recorder site gets a random intercept.

```{r fp-data}
thresholds <- c(custom = 0.40, birdnet = 0.10)
zs <- function(v) as.numeric(scale(v))

curiango_data <- function(classifier) {
  m <- curiango$minutes
  auto <- data.frame(site_night = m$site_night,
                     y = as.integer(m[[paste0("conf_", classifier)]] >=
                                      thresholds[[classifier]]),
                     bio = zs(m$bio), aci = zs(m$aci), recorder = m$site)
  n <- curiango$nights
  sites <- data.frame(site_night = n$site_night, temp = zs(n$temp),
                      rh = zs(n$rh), moon = zs(log(n$moon)))
  ver <- data.frame(site_night = curiango$verified$site_night,
                    y = curiango$verified$y)
  fp_data(auto, sites, ver, site = "site_night", recorder = "recorder")
}

d_custom <- curiango_data("custom")
d_custom
```

## Fitting

For each classifier we fit three models that differ only in the
false-positive process: a standard occupancy model that takes every
automated detection at face value (`fp = NULL`), a constant false-positive
rate (`fp = ~ 1`), and a rate that depends on the same three covariates as
occupancy (`fp = ~ temp + rh + moon`). The code is shown but not run; the
six fits took about an hour each with crywolf 1.0.0, one core per chain.
Later versions can split each chain among cores: with
`threads_per_chain = 4`, the constant-rate fit of the custom classifier took
16.5 minutes on an 18-core laptop, with the same posterior.

```{r fit, eval = FALSE}
fp_models <- list(standard = NULL, constant = ~ 1,
                  covariates = ~ temp + rh + moon)
m <- fp_occu(d_custom, occ = ~ temp + rh + moon, det = ~ bio + aci,
             fp = fp_models$constant, random_recorder = TRUE,
             threads_per_chain = 1, seed = 1)
```

## Convergence

Before reading any estimate, check the sampler. The table gives, for each
fit, the number of divergent transitions, the largest R-hat, and the
smallest bulk and tail effective sample sizes over all parameters (4 chains
of 1000 draws).

```{r convergence, echo = FALSE}
conv <- purrr::map(fits, function(f) {
  data.frame(classifier = classifiers[[f$classifier]],
             model = model_labels[[f$model]],
             divergences = f$diagnostics$divergences,
             max_rhat = round(f$diagnostics$max_rhat, 3),
             min_ess_bulk = round(f$diagnostics$min_ess_bulk),
             min_ess_tail = round(f$diagnostics$min_ess_tail),
             minutes = round(f$minutes))
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
knitr::kable(conv)
```

## How often does each classifier err?

In the constant-rate model, `p10_ref` is the probability that a recording
from a night without the species is a detection.

```{r p10, echo = FALSE}
p10 <- purrr::map(fits[grepl("_constant$", names(fits))], function(f) {
  r <- row_of(f, "p10_ref")
  data.frame(classifier = classifiers[[f$classifier]],
             p10 = pct(r$mean), lower = pct(r$lower), upper = pct(r$upper))
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
knitr::kable(p10, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r p10-night, include = FALSE}
k_night <- mean(table(curiango$minutes$site_night))
p10_mean <- purrr::map_dbl(fits[c("custom_constant", "birdnet_constant")],
                           function(f) row_of(f, "p10_ref")$mean)
night_fp <- 1 - (1 - p10_mean)^k_night
v <- curiango$verified
neg <- match(paste(v$site_night, v$time)[v$y == 0],
             paste(curiango$minutes$site_night, curiango$minutes$time))
raw_fp <- c(custom = mean(curiango$minutes$conf_custom[neg] >= 0.40),
            birdnet = mean(curiango$minutes$conf_birdnet[neg] >= 0.10))
```

The custom classifier errs about once in 300 recordings from a night without
the species, BirdNET about once in 50. A site-night has on average
`r round(k_night)` recordings, so a night without the species would still
produce at least one false detection with probability
`r sprintf("%.2f", night_fp[1])` (custom) or `r sprintf("%.2f", night_fp[2])`
(BirdNET). This is why the standard occupancy model, which reads every
detection as presence, estimates a much higher occupancy below.

The custom estimate agrees with the 0.31% (95% CrI 0.29–0.33%) of Piatti et
al. (2026). Their BirdNET estimate, 0.43% (0.40–0.46%), is about four times
lower than ours, a difference that matches the definition of the
occasion. Piatti et al. (2026) used each detection window of the source
table as an occasion; here the occasion is the one-minute recording, a
detection when any of its windows reaches the threshold. A minute has
between 1 and 20 windows in the source table. When the custom classifier
detects the species, its score repeats across all windows of the minute;
the BirdNET score is usually non-zero in only one of them. Counted by
window, BirdNET detections are therefore diluted: in the public deposit,
7.3% of the minutes but only 1.6% of the windows hold a BirdNET detection,
a ratio of 4.6, close to the ratio of 4.4 between the two estimates. The
custom classifier is not diluted in this way (1.8% of minutes, 3.3% of
windows), which is consistent with the agreement of the two custom
estimates. The two analyses also differ in their random effects, so the
match is approximate. A false-positive rate is a rate per occasion and
must be read with its occasion: per
one-minute recording, BirdNET at a threshold of 0.10 errs about once in 50
recordings.

The annotated recordings agree with the per-minute rates: of the
`r length(neg)` annotated recordings without the species,
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * raw_fp[["birdnet"]])` reached the BirdNET
threshold, against `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * raw_fp[["custom"]])` for the
custom classifier. These raw shares are not estimates of the false-positive
rate, because many of these recordings come from nights when the species was
present, but they give a sense of its order of magnitude.

## Occupancy with and without false positives

```{r occ, echo = FALSE}
occ <- purrr::map(fits, function(f) {
  t <- f$table[grepl("^occ_", f$table$variable), ]
  data.frame(classifier = classifiers[[f$classifier]],
             model = model_labels[[f$model]],
             parameter = t$variable,
             estimate = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", t$mean, t$lower, t$upper))
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
occ$model <- factor(occ$model, model_labels)
occ <- stats::reshape(occ, idvar = c("classifier", "parameter"),
                      timevar = "model", direction = "wide")
names(occ) <- sub("^estimate\\.", "", names(occ))
knitr::kable(occ, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Posterior means and 95% intervals of the occupancy coefficients (logit scale, standardized covariates).")
```

Ignoring false positives inflates occupancy: the intercept, the logit of the
probability that the species calls on an average night, drops by about one
unit with the custom classifier and by more than 1.5 units with BirdNET once
false positives are modelled. The covariate effects keep their signs.
Calling activity declines with humidity and with temperature in every
model, as Piatti et al. (2026) found, and the temperature effect roughly
doubles once false positives are modelled. The effect of moonlight is small
and its interval includes zero in most models.

## Does the false-positive rate track the environment?

The third model lets the false-positive rate depend on temperature,
humidity, and moonlight. Its coefficients are on the logit scale, per
standard deviation of each covariate:

```{r fp, echo = FALSE}
fpc <- purrr::map(fits[grepl("_covariates$", names(fits))], function(f) {
  t <- f$table[grepl("^fp_", f$table$variable) & f$table$variable != "fp_gap", ]
  data.frame(classifier = classifiers[[f$classifier]], parameter = t$variable,
             mean = round(t$mean, 2), lower = round(t$lower, 2),
             upper = round(t$upper, 2))
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
knitr::kable(fpc, row.names = FALSE)
```

For both classifiers the false-positive rate falls on humid nights
(`fp_rh` below zero), so false positives are more frequent where the species
is also more active. This is the situation in which a constant rate can
bias the occupancy slope (`vignette("calibration", package = "crywolf")`).
Here the humidity effect on occupancy changes little when the rate is
allowed to depend on humidity, by less than a fifth of its value, so the
constant-rate estimates of the occupancy effects are not far off. The
effects of temperature and moonlight on the false-positive rate are small or
uncertain.

## Model comparison

All three models of a classifier use the same automated and verified data,
so their leave-one-site-night-out cross-validation scores are comparable.

```{r loo}
purrr::map(c("custom", "birdnet"), function(cl) {
  l <- purrr::map(fits[paste(cl, names(model_labels), sep = "_")], "loo")
  names(l) <- model_labels
  loo::loo_compare(l)
}) |> setNames(classifiers)
```

Modelling false positives improves the expected predictive accuracy by
440 (custom) and more than 1200 (BirdNET) units of `elpd`. Letting the rate depend
on the covariates helps further for BirdNET (a difference of about three
standard errors) but not clearly for the custom classifier. One site-night
in each BirdNET model has a Pareto *k* above 0.7, so those comparisons rest
on a slightly less reliable approximation.

## Posterior predictive checks

`fp_ppc()` compares the number of automated detections per site-night with
replicates from the posterior, using the Freeman-Tukey discrepancy. A
Bayesian p-value near 0 or 1 means that the model does not reproduce the
data.

```{r ppc, echo = FALSE}
ppc <- purrr::map(fits, function(f) {
  data.frame(classifier = classifiers[[f$classifier]],
             model = model_labels[[f$model]],
             p_value = round(f$ppc$p_value, 3))
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
knitr::kable(ppc, row.names = FALSE)
```

No model reproduces the counts of detections per site-night, including
those with false positives, in line with Piatti et al. (2026), where no
model showed adequate fit at this level. A likely reason, which we have not
tested here, is that calls cluster within a night: a calling bird is
recorded in runs of consecutive minutes, so detections are more dispersed
among nights than independent occasions allow. The estimates above should
therefore be read as a comparison among models, not as well-calibrated
absolute values; a model with dependence among occasions is beyond the
scope of crywolf.

## Predicted occupancy

The predictions hold the other covariates at their means and are shown on
the original scale of each covariate.

```{r pred, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Predicted probability that the species calls on a night, with 95% intervals, for each classifier and model."}
n <- curiango$nights
unscale <- list(temp = c(mean(n$temp), stats::sd(n$temp)),
                rh = c(mean(n$rh), stats::sd(n$rh)),
                moon = c(mean(log(n$moon)), stats::sd(log(n$moon))))
observed <- list(temp = range(n$temp), rh = range(n$rh), moon = range(n$moon))
pred <- purrr::map(fits, function(f) {
  p <- f$pred_occ
  p$x <- purrr::map2_dbl(p$covariate, p$value,
                         function(v, z) z * unscale[[v]][2] + unscale[[v]][1])
  p$x[p$covariate == "moon"] <- exp(p$x[p$covariate == "moon"])
  keep <- purrr::map2_lgl(p$covariate, p$x, function(v, x)
    x >= observed[[v]][1] && x <= observed[[v]][2])
  p <- p[keep, ]
  p$classifier <- classifiers[[f$classifier]]
  p$model <- model_labels[[f$model]]
  p
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
pred$covariate <- factor(pred$covariate, c("temp", "rh", "moon"),
                         c("Temperature (°C)", "Relative humidity (%)",
                           "Lunar illumination"))
pred$model <- factor(pred$model, model_labels)
ggplot2::ggplot(pred, ggplot2::aes(x, estimate, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
                       alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(classifier ~ covariate, scales = "free_x") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Occupancy probability", colour = "Model",
                fill = "Model") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Each curve is drawn only over the range of the covariate observed in the
data.

observational error occur: non-detection and species misidentification.
